title: Binsfeld's Tractatus: Trier Chancellor Systematizes German Prosecution
description: Peter Binsfeld, suffragan bishop of Trier and a key figure in that territory's persecutions, published Tractatus de Confessionibus Maleficorum et Sagarum in 1589 as a systematic defense and guide to witch prosecution. Binsfeld argued that confessions obtained under torture were reliable evidence because the devil would not permit witches to confess falsely, and that the testimony of accused witches against their accomplices was sufficient for conviction. His treatise provided both theological justification and practical procedural guidance for the chain-reaction persecution pattern: extracting from each accused the names of others seen at sabbaths, then prosecuting those named. The Tractatus went through multiple editions and was widely used in German territories alongside the Malleus.
historiographical_note: Wolfgang Behringer's Witches and Witch-Hunts (2004) analyzes the role of texts like Binsfeld's Tractatus in standardizing prosecution procedure across German territories. The treatise's argument that torture-produced confessions were reliable — because Satan would not permit false confessions — represents the kind of circular theological reasoning that critics like Friedrich Spee later targeted.
source_method: Binsfeld, Tractatus de Confessionibus Maleficorum et Sagarum (1589); secondary scholarship on German demonology
